events.title: Congress passed the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution
events.summary: In response to discriminatory practices following the Civil War, Congress passed the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868, which guaranteed that no state could make or enforce laws that abridge the privileges or immunities of citizens, nor deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process.
events.why_relevant: The Fourteenth Amendment was a landmark legal protection for civil rights, ensuring equal protection under the law for all citizens.

events.title: Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution
events.summary: In 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, which prohibited human enslavement except as punishment for crime and granted Congress the power to enforce the amendment. This amendment was a significant step in the legal abolition of slavery in the United States.
events.why_relevant: The Thirteenth Amendment marked a crucial legal shift towards equality and the protection of human rights in the United States.

events.summary: The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Zorn v. Linton and reversed the Second Circuit's denial of qualified immunity to Sergeant Jacob Zorn. Zorn had used a rear wristlock on Shela Linton, a nonviolent protester engaged in a sit-in at Vermont's state capitol, causing her arm injuries and psychological trauma. The Second Circuit held that prior precedent clearly established the unconstitutionality of such force. SCOTUS reversed, holding that the prior case (Amnesty America v. events.basis: The Second Circuit reversed. It held that its decision in Amnesty America v. West Hartford, 361 F. 3d 113 (2004), clearly established that the 'gratuitous' use of a rear wristlock on a protester passively resisting arrest constitutes excessive force... We reverse.

events.summary: An Air Canada Express flight collided with a Port Authority fire truck at LaGuardia Airport on Sunday, killing pilots MacKenzie Gunther and Antoine Forest and injuring 41 others. NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System shows pilots filed multiple safety complaints months before the crash, citing air traffic control failures, inadequate guidance on aircraft separation, and operational stress. The air traffic controller who cleared the fire truck later acknowledged error, stating he had been "dealing with an emergency earlier" and "messed up." Investigators are examining systemic factors including controller shortages, aging equipment, and federal personnel cuts.

events.title: Joint Base Andrews failed to disclose jet fuel leak to Maryland regulators
events.summary: Personnel at Joint Base Andrews discovered they were missing tens of thousands of gallons of jet fuel. The base's fuel system had failed a leak safety test in early December. In January and February, it had lost about 10,000 gallons of jet fuel, but staff believed the leak was contained to the base. On March 23, someone on the base spotted oil on the freshwater creek that starts on the sprawling Prince George's County, Maryland military facility. That day DOD finally called the state. For an unknown period of time, jet fuel had been spilling into the Piscataway Creek, which feeds into the Potomac River. Late March was the first time the state of Maryland had heard of any issues at the base, despite strict state regulations requiring the facility to immediately disclose leaks. It took roughly two more weeks for DOD to disclose the full extent of the spillage from a second leak in the system. In all, the base has lost about 32,000 gallons of jet fuel between the two leaks.
events.why_relevant: The failure of a federal military facility to promptly disclose environmental contamination to state regulators violates state law and raises questions about federal accountability to state environmental protection requirements.
events.basis: That day DOD finally called the state. For an unknown period of time, jet fuel had been spilling into the Piscataway Creek, which feeds into the Potomac River. events.title: EPA establishes tolerance exemption for dimethylpolysiloxane in pesticide formulations
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency issued a final rule establishing an exemption from the requirement for a tolerance for methyl end-capped polydimethylsiloxane (CAS No. 63148-62-9) when used as an inert ingredient in pesticide formulations. The exemption lowers the minimum number average molecular weight threshold from 6,800 to 1,200 amu. EPA determined the polymer meets low-risk criteria and poses no appreciable risk to human health, including infants and children, from aggregate exposure through food, drinking water, and residential settings. The rule becomes effective immediately; objections and hearing requests must be filed by May 26, 2026.
events.why_relevant: This regulatory action reduces compliance burdens on pesticide manufacturers by lowering molecular weight thresholds, affecting agricultural chemical formulation standards and food safety oversight.

events.title: Complaint filed: Eagle County v. Department of the Interior (D.D.C. 1:26-cv-01039)
events.summary: Eagle County, Colorado filed a complaint in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging Department of the Interior guidance issued under President Trump's January 20, 2025 "national energy emergency" executive order. The guidance created a 14-day expedited environmental review process without public notice and comment, under which the Bureau of Land Management approved a right-of-way amendment increasing the Wildcat Loadout Facility's crude oil transloading capacity from 20,000 to 100,000 barrels per day. Eagle County alleges the guidance violates the Administrative Procedure Act, Federal Land Policy and Management Act, and National Environmental Policy Act; that no qualifying emergency existed; and that BLM failed to assess indirect effects and violated FOIA. The county seeks declaratory judgments vacating both the guidance and the approval, plus an order requiring BLM to produce FOIA records.
events.why_relevant: The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration's use of emergency procedures to bypass environmental review and public participation in energy project approvals, raising questions about executive power, administrative law compliance, and the rule of law.

The order, which took immediate effect, expands existing ethics rules to prohibit state appointees from using nonpublic information to enrich themselves or family members on prediction market bets. Newsom framed the order as a response to concerns about rampant insider trading on fast-growing platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket. In his statement, Newsom criticized the Trump administration's failure to enforce ethical standards that would prevent government insiders from abusing prediction markets.
events.why_relevant: The executive order establishes state-level ethics enforcement against insider trading on prediction markets, addressing a gap in federal oversight and setting a standard for preventing government officials from profiting from nonpublic information.
events.federal_nexus: The order responds to federal-level ethical failures and insider profiteering in the Trump administration.
events.basis: Gavin Newsom signed an executive order banning appointed state officials with insider information from betting on prediction markets.

events.title: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth blocked promotion of four Army officers to one-star general rank
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth blocked the promotion of four Army officers to one-star general rank, a highly unusual move that prompted senior military officials to question whether the officers were being singled out based on race or gender. Two of the officers targeted are Black and two are women on a promotion list of approximately three dozen officers, most of whom are white men. Hegseth had pressed Army leaders, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, for months to remove the officers' names. Driscoll repeatedly refused, citing the officers' decades-long records of exemplary service. Hegseth unilaterally struck the officers' names from the list, though it is unclear whether he has legal authority to do so. The list was under White House review for Senate approval.
events.why_relevant: The Defense Secretary's unilateral removal of qualified officers from a promotion list based on apparent race and gender discrimination undermines military merit-based advancement and raises constitutional concerns about equal protection and civil rights.
events.basis: Hegseth is blocking the promotion of 4 Army officers to be one-star generals, a highly unusual move that has prompted some senior military officials to question whether the officers are being singled out because of their race or gender.
